name: Jerome

seo.title: St Jerome: the Bible translator's temper, quotes and feast days
seo.description: Who St Jerome was, in plain words: the dream, the desert, his Bible from the Hebrew, his temper, his best lines and his feast days East and West.

person.birthPlace: Stridon, on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia

band.lede: The scholar-monk behind the Latin Bible, and one of the fiercest letter-writers in Christian history.

picture.alt: An old man with a long white beard and close-cropped white hair looks straight out at the viewer, dressed in a red cardinal's cape, both hands on the open pages of a large book.
picture.credit: Saint Jerome as Scholar, El Greco, about 1610. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. Public domain. The cardinal's robes are the painter's: there were no cardinals in Jerome's day.
picture.creator: El Greco

card.line: The scholar-monk behind the Latin Bible, and one of the fiercest letter-writers in Christian history.

who: Jerome was a scholar and monk. He revised the Latin Gospels for Pope Damasus, then spent 15 years at Bethlehem translating the Old Testament from Hebrew. His work lies behind the Latin Bible later called the Vulgate. He knew Latin, Greek and Hebrew. He was devout, brilliant and quick to anger, and he fought his opponents in blistering letters.

roles.name: Priest
roles.line: On condition he stayed a monk

lines: A guest who stayed six months at Bethlehem said no one dared compare himself with him
The books of the Hebrew Bible, into Latin
numbers.src: Catholic Encyclopedia, Latin Versions of the Bible

He spoke it in Latin to a secretary
About that many, across half a century
Loved in the Renaissance, like Augustine's *Confessions*

The last life is his own

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 347. Older books say 340 to 345. At Stridon, a town “on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia”. The Goths later destroyed it, and no one knows exactly where it stood. His parents were Christians and well off.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: At Stridon, then at school in **Rome** from about 12, under the grammarian Donatus. He was baptised in Rome, about 366.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **30 September 420**, at Bethlehem. His last year is believed to have been one long illness. Some sources say he died in 419.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At Bethlehem, near the cave of the Nativity, beside Paula and Eustochium. His body was later said to have been moved to Rome, to St Mary Major. The OCA says no one now knows where his relics are.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Eusebius Hieronymus**, his Latin name. **Jerome of Stridon**. **Blessed Jerome**, in the Russian Church. **The Venerable Jerome**, in Greek.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics and Orthodox. For Catholics he is a **Doctor of the Church**. Anglicans and Lutherans remember him too.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: Translators, Bible scholars, librarians, students and archaeologists, says *Britannica*. The UN keeps his feast day, 30 September, as **International Translation Day**.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: With a lion at his side. In a cardinal's red hat and robes, or with the hat at his feet. Or kneeling in the wilderness, beating his breast with a stone.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Most of the Latin Bible later called the **Vulgate**. Also commentaries on the prophets and on other books of the Bible, the lives of three hermits, 135 short lives of Christian writers, fierce answers to his opponents, and about 120 letters that survive.

facts.label: Pronounced
facts.text: **juh-ROHM**, or JERR-um. His Latin name, Hieronymus, is **hy-uh-RON-uh-mus**.

portrait.alt: An icon on a gold ground: a grey-bearded Jerome with a halo kneels in a cave mouth, a stone in his hand, before a crucifix, with a lion beside him, a red cardinal's hat on the ground and a church on the hill behind.
portrait.credit: Saint Jerome praying before the crucifix, Venetian-Cretan icon, 15th century. Museo nazionale di Ravenna. Photo: Sailko, Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
portrait.caption: An icon painted in Venetian Crete in the 1400s. He kneels before the cross with a stone in his hand, with his lion and the red hat. He wrote of beating his breast. The stone is the painters'. Museo nazionale di Ravenna. Public domain.

typeNote: Serious here means he took everything to heart, grief and argument alike. Restless fits a man who, a visitor said, never stopped reading and writing.

west.text: In the **1916 Roman Martyrology**: his body moved from Bethlehem to St Mary Major in Rome.
**Catholic** memorial. Also the **Church of England** (a Commemoration), the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: **OCA** and **Greek** churches. The Greek calendar gives the same day to the prophet Amos and to Augustine. The **Russian Church** keeps it on the old calendar: that is 28 June on today's calendar.

feasts.note: The West keeps 30 September, the day he died. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so 15 June falls on 28 June.

traits.title: a fighter, and said so
traits.text: In a war of words, he wrote, “I stand in the thick of the fray, my life in constant danger.” He owned his temper: “I will frankly admit that my indignation overpowers me.” He gave his opponents nicknames. Vigilantius, whose name means Wakeful, became Dormitantius, the Sleepy one.

cite.text: Letter 48, section 13; Letter 109, section 3; Against Vigilantius, section 1

traits.title: never without a book
traits.text: A visitor who stayed with him for six months said, “he takes no rest day or night; he is perpetually either reading or writing something.” He wrote so often to Paula and her daughter that he could not count the letters, “for I write daily”.

cite.text: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues, Dialogue I, chapter 9; Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 135

traits.title: not for sale
traits.text: When Rome turned against him, he asked, “Have I taken any one's money? Have I not disdained all gifts, whether small or great?” The Episcopal Church's calendar book, which is frank about his faults, says he never sought high office in the Church.

cite.text: Letter 45, section 2; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

traits.title: tender in grief
traits.text: His old friend Heliodorus lost his nephew Nepotian, a young priest Jerome loved. Jerome wrote, “my eyes fill with tears, my grief returns, and I can think of nothing but his death.”

cite.text: Letter 60, section 1

traits.title: funny about himself
traits.text: He could laugh at his own old face: “my head is gray, my brow is furrowed, a dewlap like that of an ox hangs from my chin”. Grey and bald, he still dreamed he was a curly-haired schoolboy about to make a speech, “and, when I wake, I congratulate myself on escaping the peril of making a speech.”

cite.text: Letter 52, section 1; Apology against Rufinus, Book 1, section 30

said.lede: People argued about him. Friend and foe agreed he was brilliant.

quotes.q: The heretics hate him, because he never desists from attacking them; the clerics hate him, because he assails their life and crimes. But beyond doubt, all the good admire and love him.
quotes.who: Postumianus, who stayed six months with him at Bethlehem, in Sulpicius Severus's *Dialogues*

cite.text: Dialogues, Dialogue I, chapter 9

quotes.q: …we bless God that to yourself, to us, to all who read your works, He has given you as you are.
quotes.who: Augustine of Hippo, who never met him, writing to him in 397

cite.text: Augustine, Letter 40, section 1

quotes.q: Jerome, the Teacher of the Catholics, whose writings shine like divine lamps throughout the whole world…
quotes.who: John Cassian, about ten years after Jerome died

cite.text: On the Incarnation of the Lord, Book 7, chapter 26

quotes.q: A certain Jerome, a priest, distinguished Latin writer and cultivated scholar as he was, showed qualities of temper so disastrous that they threw into the shade his splendid achievements.
quotes.who: Palladius, a friend of Jerome's enemy Rufinus, writing about 420

cite.text: Lausiac History, chapter 36

moments.title: A student in Rome
moments.text: As a small boy at home, he said, he had to be “dragged like a captive from my grandmother's lap” to his lessons. At about 12 he went on to school in Rome, under the grammarian Donatus. There he built up a library “with great care and toil”, and there he was baptised, about 366.

cite.text: Apology against Rufinus, Book 1, section 30; Letter 22, section 30; Britannica

moments.title: The dream
moments.text: He still could not give up his books. He would fast, he said, “only that I might afterwards read Cicero.” Then in Lent he fell ill with a fever, and they began to prepare his funeral. He saw himself dragged before the Judge. Asked who he was, he said, “I am a Christian.” The answer came: “Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero and not of Christ.” He was flogged, and he swore never again to read pagan books. He insisted “this was no sleep nor idle dream”, for he woke with his shoulders “black and blue”. Years later his old friend Rufinus called him a perjurer for still quoting the classics. Jerome answered that his oath was “a promise for the future, not the abolition of my memory of the past”.

cite.text: Letter 22, section 30; Apology against Rufinus, Book 1, section 30

moments.title: Alone in the desert
moments.text: He went to live as a hermit in the Syrian desert, burnt by the sun and half starved. His mind still went back to Rome: “I often found myself amid bevies of girls.” Years later he told it plainly to a young woman: “I do not blush to avow my abject misery.” To tame his thoughts, he asked a monk who had been a Jew to teach him Hebrew. After Cicero's smooth Latin, he had to learn to say “words both harsh and guttural”. Long after, he wrote, “I thank the Lord that from this seed of learning sown in bitterness I now cull sweet fruits.”

cite.text: Letter 22, section 7; Letter 125, section 12

moments.title: A priest, on his terms
moments.text: Bishop Paulinus of Antioch wanted to ordain him. Jerome agreed only if he could stay a monk. “Did I ask to be ordained by you?” he told the bishop. He was made a priest, and he lived as a monk to the end.

cite.text: Against John of Jerusalem, section 41

moments.title: The Pope's secretary
moments.text: Pope Damasus used him to answer letters from councils East and West, and set him to revise the Latin Gospels. Jerome taught the Bible and Hebrew to a circle of Roman women, Marcella and Paula among them. Then Paula's daughter Blaesilla died of a fever. She was twenty. At her funeral, people in the crowd whispered that fasting had killed her, and blamed the monks: “Why do we not stone them or hurl them into the Tiber?” Damasus died in December 384. People called Jerome “an infamous turncoat, a slippery knave”, and gossip linked him with Paula. His only crime, he wrote, was being a man: “my sex is my one crime”. In August 385 he sailed for the East.

cite.text: Letter 123, section 10; Letter 39, section 6; Letter 45, sections 2 and 6

moments.title: Settling at Bethlehem
moments.text: He settled at Bethlehem with Paula and Eustochium. Paula built a monastery for men, which Jerome led, and convents for women, and a house for pilgrims. Apart from short journeys, he lived there for his last 34 years. His great work was done there.

cite.text: Britannica; Letter 108

moments.title: Rome falls
moments.text: News came that Alaric's Goths had taken Rome. “My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance.” Soldiers beat his old friend Marcella for gold she did not have, and she died a few days later. Then refugees poured into Bethlehem. He put aside his commentary on Ezekiel to look after them: “the quiet of the monastery has been changed into the bustle of a guest house”.

cite.text: Letter 127, sections 12 to 14; Commentary on Ezekiel, prefaces to Books 3 and 7

moments.title: Fire at the monastery
moments.text: Supporters of Pelagius, whose teaching Jerome had attacked, raided the Bethlehem monasteries. Augustine reports what he heard: they beat the monks and nuns, killed a deacon and burned the buildings. Jerome escaped “in the shelter of a well-defended fortress”.

cite.text: Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapter 66

extras.title: The Bible he translated
extras.lede: The Latin Bible later called the Vulgate is mostly his work. He worked on it, on and off, from 382 to 405.

items.title: Back to the Hebrew
items.text: In 382 Pope Damasus set him to revise the Latin Gospels, and he finished them about 383. Next he revised parts of the Old Testament from the Greek, the old translation the Church used. Then he decided the Greek was not good enough and went back to the Hebrew. He worked through it at Bethlehem, from 390 to 405.

cite.text: Britannica, Vulgate; Catholic Encyclopedia, Latin Versions of the Bible

items.title: Lessons by night
items.text: Back in Jerusalem and Bethlehem he paid a Jewish teacher, Baraninas, who came only after dark, like Nicodemus, for fear of other Jews. For the book of Tobit, written in Aramaic, he found a man who knew both languages. He called the result “one day's hasty labour”.
items.quote: What trouble and expense it cost me to get Baraninas to teach me under cover of night.

cite.text: Letter 84, section 3; his preface to Tobit

items.title: The ivy uproar
items.text: At Oea, in North Africa, a bishop read out Jerome's new Jonah in church. Where the old Latin had Jonah sit under a gourd, Jerome had put ivy. The people made such an uproar that the bishop changed it back. Augustine told Jerome, who replied that the Hebrew named neither plant. He had put ivy, he said, “that I might not differ from all other translators”.
items.quote: The man was compelled to correct your version in that passage as if it had been falsely translated, as he desired not to be left without a congregation—a calamity which he narrowly escaped.

cite.text: Augustine, Letter 71, section 5; Jerome, Letter 75, section 22

items.title: What became of it
items.text: It was not taken up at once. From the middle of the 500s, whole Bibles built on his work came into common use. His translator of 1893 called it “the Bible of the Middle Ages”.

cite.text: Britannica, Vulgate; Fremantle's introduction to Jerome's works, 1893

items.title: A line still quoted
items.text: It comes at the start of his commentary on Isaiah: {la|ignoratio Scripturarum, ignoratio Christi est}. In plain English, not to know the Scriptures is not to know Christ. Pope Leo XIII quoted it in 1893, in his letter on the study of Scripture.

cite.text: Commentary on Isaiah, prologue, in Latin; Leo XIII, Providentissimus Deus

extras.title: Hard questions
extras.lede: Parts of what he wrote are hard to read today. Here they are, in his own words and his critics'.

items.title: Marriage and virginity
items.text: He put virginity far above marriage, and said so bluntly: “I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins.” On Paul's words he wrote, “If it is good not to touch a woman, it is bad to touch one.” His friends in Rome thought his book against Jovinian went too far. Pammachius pulled copies of it, and Jerome admitted people called him excessive “in depreciation of marriage”. He answered that Paul laid down a rule, while he himself only asked a question: “He defines a dogma, I hazard an inquiry.” The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1910 says his hard words on marriage were criticised in his own day, and that he “has given no satisfactory explanation” for them.

cite.text: Letter 22, section 20; Against Jovinian, Book 1, section 7; Letters 48 and 49; Catholic Encyclopedia

items.title: Paula
items.text: Palladius, a friend of Rufinus and no friend of Jerome, wrote that Paula “was able to surpass all”, but that Jerome “hindered her by his jealousy”. The Episcopal Church's calendar sees it the other way: Paula and her daughter were his colleagues, and without them there would be no Vulgate.

cite.text: Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 41; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, Paula and Eustochium

items.title: Hard in grief and in argument
items.text: When Blaesilla died, he told her weeping mother, “Yours are detestable tears, sacrilegious tears, unbelieving tears.” He held that “there is no cruelty in regard for God's honour.” He defended his way of debating: in a war of words, he wrote, “one argues as one pleases, saying one thing while one means another.” The Episcopal Church's calendar book names his short temper, his pride in his learning and his extreme promotion of self-denial. It adds that he was at times candid about his failings.

cite.text: Letter 39, section 6; Letter 109, section 3; Letter 48, section 13; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

items.title: On the Jews
items.text: He learned his Hebrew from Jewish teachers, and defended it: “can anyone find fault with me for having had a Jew as a teacher?” In the same passage he wrote, “If it is expedient to hate any men and to loath any race, I have a strange dislike to those of the circumcision. For up to the present day they persecute our Lord Jesus Christ in the synagogues of Satan.” The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1904 gives both sides. Its article on him is by the scholars Crawford Howell Toy and Samuel Krauss. It says he went on studying with Jews through his years in Palestine. No other Church Father, it says, passes on so many Jewish traditions so faithfully. Then it says: “Jerome was no friend to the Jews, although he owed them much.” He scolded and cursed them, it adds, and he “even uses against them both the books that he has cunningly obtained from them and the knowledge he has derived therefrom”.

cite.text: Letter 84, section 3; Jewish Encyclopedia (1904), volume 7, article on Jerome by Crawford Howell Toy and Samuel Krauss

words.note: All from his own letters and books, in W. H. Fremantle's translation of 1893.

feature.q: The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken.
feature.ctx: Written at Bethlehem, on hearing that the Goths had taken Rome. In Latin, {la|Capitur Urbs, quae totum cepit orbem.}

cite.text: Letter 127, to Principia, section 12

quotes.q: Always have some work on hand, that the devil may find you busy.
quotes.who: Advice to a young monk. In Latin, {la|Facito aliquid operis, ut te semper diabolus inveniat occupatum.}

cite.text: Letter 125, to Rusticus, section 11

quotes.q: The art of interpreting the scriptures is the only one of which all men everywhere claim to be masters.
quotes.who: On people who think the Bible needs no study.

cite.text: Letter 53, to Paulinus, section 7

quotes.q: Of two imperfect things holy rusticity is better than sinful eloquence.
quotes.who: From a great stylist, to a young priest.

cite.text: Letter 52, to Nepotian, section 9

quotes.q: Almost all bodily excellences alter with age, and while wisdom alone increases all things else decay.

cite.text: Letter 52, to Nepotian, section 3

quotes.q: When the stomach is full, it is easy to talk of fasting.

cite.text: Letter 58, to Paulinus, section 2

quotes.q: What is praiseworthy is not to have been at Jerusalem but to have lived a good life while there.
quotes.who: From a man who lived at Bethlehem.

cite.text: Letter 58, to Paulinus, section 2

quotes.q: The scars of others should teach us caution.

cite.text: Letter 54, to Furia, section 13

quotes.q: I beseech you, reader, whoever you may be, to remember Jerome the sinner. He, if God would give him his choice, would much sooner take Paul's tunic with his merits, than the purple of kings with their punishment.
quotes.who: The last lines of an early book, written in the desert.

cite.text: Life of Paul the First Hermit, section 18

myths.claim: He pulled a thorn from a lion's paw, and the lion stayed on at his monastery.
myths.truth: A legend that grew up after his death. His translator of 1893 thought his pictures of desert life gave rise to it. The art historian Anna Jameson thought the lion came first, as a sign of his fiery nature, with “the legend invented to explain the symbol”.

cite.text: Fremantle, 1893; Jameson, Sacred and Legendary Art, 1870

myths.claim: He was a cardinal. That is why painters give him the red hat and robes.
myths.truth: There were no cardinals in his day. He was a priest, and for a few years a pope's secretary. As Jameson put it in 1870, “there is no historical authority for making St. Jerome a cardinal”.

cite.text: Jameson, Sacred and Legendary Art; Letter 123, section 10

myths.claim: “Good, better, best, never let it rest, til your good is better, and your better best.”
myths.truth: A fact-checker searched his works in English and found nothing like it. The rhyme was in print by 1897, with no link to him. It seems to have been pinned on him only in this century.

cite.text: Fauxtations, 2016

myths.claim: He made up the saying about looking a gift horse in the mouth.
myths.truth: He used it, but as a proverb everyone knew: {la|ut vulgare proverbium est}. His Latin, in the preface to his commentary on Ephesians, is {la|equi dentes inspicere donati}, to inspect the teeth of a horse given as a gift.

cite.text: Commentary on Ephesians, preface, in Latin

myths.claim: He translated the whole Latin Bible himself.
myths.truth: He revised the Gospels and translated most of the Old Testament from Hebrew. The rest of the New Testament came from older Latin versions, which he may have lightly revised. Some books found only in the Greek Old Testament also came in from the older Latin.

cite.text: Britannica, Vulgate; Catholic Encyclopedia, Latin Versions of the Bible

myths.claim: “Vulgate” means the Bible in the language of the common people.
myths.truth: The name comes from {la|editio vulgata}, the “common version”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says the name marks its common use. Until the 600s the same name belonged to the older Latin Bible. It was firmly fixed to his only in the 1200s.

cite.text: Britannica, Vulgate; Catholic Encyclopedia, Latin Versions of the Bible

stood.lede: Each line is his own. The line on riches is our translation of his Latin: he calls it a common saying and agrees with it. The line on family he wrote as a young man. Years later he said he had “decked it out a good deal with the flourishes of the schools”.

circle.name: Paula
circle.text: A Roman noblewoman who followed him to Bethlehem and built its monasteries. She learned Hebrew so well that “she could chant the psalms in Hebrew”. His tribute to her is Letter 108. She died in 404.

cite.text: Letter 108, section 27; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

circle.name: Eustochium
circle.text: Paula's daughter. His famous Letter 22, on virginity, was written to her. She led the convent after her mother, and died about 418. Her death, he wrote, wore him down.

cite.text: Letter 22; Augustine, Letter 202

circle.name: Marcella
circle.text: A Roman widow who studied the Bible with him. She would not take his answers on trust, “but on the contrary would dispute them; not, however, for argument's sake but to learn the answers”. After he left Rome, people went to her to settle questions on Scripture.

cite.text: Letter 127, section 7

circle.name: Paulinian
circle.text: His brother, twenty years younger. He sailed east with Jerome in 385. In 394 Bishop Epiphanius made him a priest to serve the Bethlehem monks, against his will. Epiphanius told his deacons “to seize him and to stop his mouth”.

cite.text: Fremantle, 1893; Epiphanius, in Jerome's Letter 51, section 1

circle.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
circle.text: His teacher at Constantinople. Asked to explain a hard phrase in Luke, the second-first Sabbath, Gregory joked that he would do it in church, “and there, when all the people applaud me, you will be forced against your will to know what you do not know at all.”

cite.text: Letter 52, section 8

circle.name: Augustine of Hippo
circle.text: They wrote to each other from about 394 to 419 and never met. The early letters were sharp. Jerome told the younger man, “do not because you are young challenge a veteran in the field of Scripture”, and added, “The tired ox treads with a firmer step.” The last letters were warm: “You are renowned throughout the whole world.”

cite.text: Augustine's Letters 68, 195 and 202

circle.name: Rufinus of Aquileia
circle.text: His closest friend when young. Jerome once wrote to him, “The friendship which can cease has never been real.” They fell out over Origen and attacked each other in books for years. Augustine asked, “where is the friend who may not be feared as possibly a future enemy, if the breach that we deplore could arise between Jerome and Rufinus?”

cite.text: Letter 3, section 6; Augustine, Letter 73, section 6

circle.name: Origen
circle.text: Jerome admired and translated him, and called him “our Christian man of brass, or, rather, man of adamant”. Then he turned against his teaching. Later he said, “I have praised the commentator but not the theologian.”

cite.text: Letter 33, section 3; Letter 84, section 2

circle.name: Ambrose of Milan
circle.text: Jerome mocked a Latin book on the Holy Spirit as “flaccid and soft, sleek and pretty”, without naming its author. Rufinus said the target was Ambrose.

cite.text: Rufinus, Apology against Jerome, Book 2

death.big: He died at Bethlehem on 30 September 420, old and ill, after 34 years there.
paras: His last known letter, of 419, went to Augustine and his friend Alypius. Eustochium had died not long before. He wrote, “I have suffered so much through the attacks of disease, and through the falling asleep of your distinguished and holy daughter Eustochium.”

His eyes were failing years before he died. Even by day he could not make out the small letters of his Hebrew books, and he needed the brothers to read him the Greek commentaries. He wrote that he shared “the suffering of the saintly Isaac”, who went blind in old age.

His last year is believed to have been one long illness. The younger Paula and Melania nursed him. No one who was there wrote down how he died, and no last words are recorded. He was buried at Bethlehem, beside Paula and Eustochium.

later.title: A later story
later.text: The detailed stories of his death and his miracles come from three letters. They claim to be by his disciple Eusebius of Cremona, by Augustine and by Cyril of Jerusalem, though Cyril had died in 386. Scholars agree they were written much later, probably in Rome late in the 1200s or early in the 1300s. Artists painted scenes from them.

cite.text: Rice, Saint Jerome in the Renaissance, 1985, as cited by textmanuscripts.com

items.k: To Augustine and Alypius, in his last known letter
items.q: I call God to witness that, if it were possible, I would take the wings of a dove and fly to be folded in your embrace.
items.ctx: He and Augustine had begun as sparring partners and ended as friends.

cite.text: Augustine, Letter 202, section 1

saint.big: Yes. Catholics and Orthodox count him a saint, and Anglicans and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: A Doctor of the Church. Memorial on 30 September
15 June. Blessed Jerome in the Russian Church
A Commemoration in the Church of England, 30 September

paras: For Catholics he is one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Church, with Ambrose, Augustine and Gregory the Great. In 1298 Pope Boniface VIII ordered the feasts of all four kept across the whole Church.
The Russian Church calls him Blessed Jerome, a title it also gives Augustine. The same Russian calendar also calls him Venerable, and a saint. The Greek calendar calls him the Venerable Jerome.
The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* gives him this entry:

quotes.q: …the decease of St. Jerome, priest and Doctor of the Church, who, excelling in all kinds of learning, imitated the life of the most approved monks, and disposed of many monstrous heresies with the sword of his doctrine. Having at length reached a very advanced age, he rested in peace, and was buried near the manger of our Lord.
quotes.who: The *Roman Martyrology*, 1916 edition, for 30 September, at Bethlehem

cite.text: The Roman Martyrology (1916)

kin.name: John Chrysostom
kin.text: A friend from his youth called him irritable, and an admiring historian says it was his nature to rebuke wrongdoing. He preached so hard against the powerful that he died in exile.

kin.name: Paul
kin.text: When the church in Jerusalem was still afraid of Saul, Barnabas brought him to the apostles. Later the two fell out over young Mark, who had once left them. Barnabas wanted to give him a second chance. Paul would not. “Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.” Years later Paul wrote, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry.”

tidbits.text: Writing to a young mother about her baby girl, he said to give her letters made of boxwood or ivory to play with, so that even her play would teach her. Old as he was, he offered to carry the child on his shoulders and teach her himself.

cite.text: Letter 107, to Laeta, sections 4 and 13

tidbits.text: Gutenberg's Bible of the 1450s was the Vulgate, the Latin Bible built on his work. In the 1500s the Council of Trent declared it the authentic version for the Catholic Church.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, Latin Versions of the Bible

tidbits.text: Before he came to know Paula's household, he wrote, all Rome sang his praises. People called him holy, humble and eloquent, and almost everyone thought him worthy to be a bishop.

cite.text: Letter 45, to Asella, section 3

gallery.alt: An engraving: Jerome, haloed and bearded, writes at a sloping desk at the back of a sunlit study. A lion and a small dog sleep in the foreground. A skull lies on the window seat, a cardinal's hat hangs on the wall and a great gourd hangs from the ceiling.
